concept.body: Definitions must use earlier words, like a tower needs a ground floor. Point, line, and plane ARE the ground floor: described (no size / two directions / every direction) but never defined. Every other term — segment, angle, circle — is built on them.

explanationVariants: Point, line, and plane are the three undefined terms — every other object is defined FROM them.
A segment is defined (part of a line between two points), so it can't be in the undefined starting stock.

widget.prompt: Which of these is one of geometry's three UNDEFINED terms?

options.label: segment
options.feedback: A segment is DEFINED — the part of a line between two endpoints. It's built from line and point.

options.label: plane
options.feedback: Plane, point, and line are the three described-not-defined starting terms.

options.label: angle
options.feedback: An angle is DEFINED — two rays sharing an endpoint. Rays come from lines and points.

options.label: circle
options.feedback: A circle is DEFINED — all points at one distance from a center. It's built from point and distance.

steps.body: Every definition uses earlier words. "A square is a rectangle with..." — but what's a rectangle? Chase definitions backward and you must stop somewhere. Geometry stops at three **undefined terms**: **point** (a location, no size), **line** (straight, extends forever both ways), **plane** (a flat surface extending forever). We describe them; we never define them. Everything else is built from these three.

widget.prompt: Drag each description to the undefined term it describes.

items.label: a location — takes up no space at all
items.feedback: "Takes up no space" is the giveaway: a line has length and a plane has area, but a point is pure location.

items.label: perfectly straight, extending forever in two opposite directions
items.feedback: "Two opposite directions" narrows it to a line — a plane spreads in EVERY direction, not just two.

items.label: perfectly flat, extending forever in every direction
items.feedback: "Every direction" is the plane's signature — a line only runs two ways.

items.label: what two distinct planes share when they intersect
items.feedback: Two walls of a room meet along a straight crease that runs forever with the planes — that's a line, not a single point.

widget.missFeedback: Match each phrase to its dimension: no size → point, two directions → line, every direction → plane.
widget.successFeedback: Sorted. No size, two directions, all directions — the three floors of geometry.

explanationVariants: Every definition needs previously defined words. Without a starting stock of undefined terms, the chain of definitions could never begin — it would be circular or infinite.
Think of a dictionary: look up every word in a definition and you eventually loop. Geometry avoids the loop by agreeing on three described-not-defined starting terms.

widget.prompt: Why does geometry leave point, line, and plane UNDEFINED?

options.label: Nobody has found good definitions for them yet
options.feedback: It's not a gap waiting to be filled — it's a deliberate choice. Definitions need earlier words, so SOME terms must be the agreed starting stock.

options.label: Every definition uses earlier terms, so some terms must come first, undefined
options.feedback: Exactly — they're the floor the whole tower of definitions stands on.

options.label: They are too simple to matter in proofs
options.feedback: They matter enormously — nearly every later definition (segment, angle, circle) is built directly from them.

options.label: They can only be understood with coordinates
options.feedback: Coordinates come later and are optional — the undefined terms are the coordinate-free starting point.

steps.body: Naming: a point gets a capital letter (point A). A line can be named by ANY two of its points with a two-way arrow on top — line AB and line BA are the same line. Points that sit on one line are **collinear**; points in one plane are **coplanar**. Order never matters for a line: it has no endpoints to start from.

widget.prompt: Points A and B sit on line ℓ. Tap every OTHER labeled point that is also on ℓ (collinear with A and B).

hotspots.label: D
hotspots.feedback: D floats above the line — from A to B the line drops steadily, and D breaks that straight path.

hotspots.label: E
hotspots.feedback: E sits below the straight path through A and B — collinear means ON the very same line.

widget.missFeedback: Sight along A and B like a ruler's edge: only one more labeled point continues that exact straight path.
widget.successFeedback: C continues the straight path through A and B — A, B, C are collinear.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents gf notation.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for gf notation must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines gf notation.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: A line has no direction and no endpoints, so the two naming points can be listed in either order: line QP is the same line as line PQ.
Contrast with a ray: ray PQ starts at P, so order matters there. For a LINE, both letters are just addresses on an endless road.

widget.prompt: Which of these is guaranteed to name the SAME object as line PQ?

options.label: line QP
options.feedback: A line runs forever both ways — either point can be listed first.

options.label: ray PQ
options.feedback: A ray starts at P and runs one way only. Line PQ has no starting point — it runs both ways.

options.label: segment PQ
options.feedback: Segment PQ stops at both P and Q. The line continues forever past each of them.

options.label: ray QP
options.feedback: Ray QP starts at Q and runs one way. The line through P and Q has no endpoint at all.

steps.body: A few facts about these terms are simply agreed to — **postulates**. Two big ones: **through any two distinct points there is exactly one line**, and **two distinct lines intersect in at most one point**. "Exactly one" is doing real work: at least one (you can always draw it) and at most one (no second line fits).
How many points can they share?

widget.prompt: Two DISTINCT lines are drawn in a plane. How many points can they have in common?

options.label: 0 or 1
options.feedback: Parallel lines share 0; intersecting lines share exactly 1. Two shared points would force the lines to be the same line.

options.label: Exactly 1 — lines always cross
options.feedback: Parallel lines never cross, so 0 is possible too.

options.label: 0, 1, or 2
options.feedback: Two shared points is impossible for DISTINCT lines: through two points there is exactly ONE line, so they'd be the same line.

options.label: Any number
options.feedback: Sharing even two points already forces the lines to coincide — the two-point postulate leaves no room for more.

hints: "Exactly one" makes two promises at once — what are they?
Promise 1: a line through the two points EXISTS. Promise 2 rules something out.
If a second, different line also passed through both points, the two lines would share two points — compare that with the intersection postulate.
explanationVariants: "Exactly one line through two points" = existence (at least one) + uniqueness (at most one). Uniqueness is what forbids a second line through the same pair.
The two postulates lock together: if two distinct lines could share two points, both "exactly one line" and "at most one intersection" would fail at once.

widget.prompt: Suppose someone claims TWO different lines both pass through points X and Y. Which postulate does the claim break?

options.label: Through any two distinct points there is exactly one line
options.feedback: The claim gives two lines through the same pair — uniqueness says at most one, so the "two" lines must really be the same line.

options.label: A line extends forever in both directions
options.feedback: Both claimed lines could extend forever and the claim would still be broken — endlessness isn't the issue; UNIQUENESS is.

options.label: Two points determine a segment
options.feedback: True but beside the point: segments are about endpoints, and the claim is about how many LINES fit through the pair.

options.label: A plane contains at least three points
options.feedback: That postulate is about planes having enough room — it says nothing about how many lines fit through two points.

takeaways: Point, line, plane are described, never defined — they're the agreed starting stock.
Lines are named by any two points, in either order; collinear = on one line.
Exactly one line through two points = it exists AND no second one does.
steps.teaser: Next: use the undefined terms to build precise definitions — segment, ray, angle, and the circle.
